title: Loading & UI States
subtitle: The data/loading/error state pattern, skeleton screens, and optimistic updates
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Without state management, API calls cause blank screens, stale data, and duplicate requests. Users don't know if their action worked. The UI looks broken during loading.
whyItExists.solution: Model every fetch operation with three states: loading (request in flight), error (request failed), and data (request succeeded). Show appropriate UI for each state. Optimistic updates make the UI feel instant by updating before the server confirms.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every API call that affects UI — data fetching on mount, form submissions, button actions.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For background sync that doesn't affect visible UI, full state machinery isn't needed. Simple fire-and-forget calls (logging, analytics) can skip the three-state pattern.

explainModes.beginner: When you make an API call, your UI can be in three states: loading (showing a spinner), error (showing an error message), or data (showing the result). Always handle all three. Show a loading indicator while waiting. Show an error message if it fails. Show the data when it succeeds. This is the most important UI pattern for any app that talks to an API.
explainModes.simple: State: { data: null, loading: false, error: null }. On fetch start: loading=true, error=null. On success: data=result, loading=false. On failure: error=err.message, loading=false. In the UI: if loading → spinner. If error → error message. If data → show data. React useEffect + useState: the standard pattern. AbortController: cancel the request if the component unmounts to avoid setting state on a dead component.
explainModes.standard: Skeleton screens: placeholder UI that matches the shape of the real content — better than spinners for perceived performance. Stale-while-revalidate: show cached data immediately while fetching fresh data in the background. Optimistic updates: update UI immediately, roll back if request fails. Mutation state: separate loading/error state for mutations (POST/PATCH/DELETE) vs queries (GET). Debounce: for search inputs — delay the API call until typing stops to avoid excessive requests.
explainModes.technical: Race condition: if a user types quickly and two requests are in-flight, the older response might arrive last and overwrite the newer data. Fix: AbortController.abort() cancels the previous request when a new one starts. Or use a requestId counter — only apply results from the latest request. React Query / SWR: libraries that handle all of this — caching, deduplication, background refresh, optimistic updates, retry, pagination. They wrap fetch() and expose { data, isLoading, error, mutate } hooks.
explainModes.deepDive: SWR (stale-while-revalidate): a caching strategy — serve cached data immediately (stale), revalidate in background, update UI when fresh data arrives. React Query (TanStack Query): full data synchronization library. Concepts: queries (reads), mutations (writes), invalidation (mark cache stale after mutation), optimistic updates via queryClient.setQueryData. Devtools: React Query Devtools shows all queries, cache state, and refetch status. Suspense mode: instead of checking isLoading, wrap in <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}> — React automatically shows fallback during data fetching (works with React Query's suspense option).

questions.question: Why should you call AbortController.abort() in the cleanup function of useEffect when fetching data?
options: It makes the fetch request faster by cancelling unnecessary work
If the component unmounts before the fetch completes, calling setState on an unmounted component causes a memory leak warning. abort() cancels the request so the .then() callbacks never fire.
AbortController is required by the Fetch API specification
It prevents the browser from caching the response
questions.explanation: When a component unmounts (user navigates away), any pending fetch requests are still in-flight. When they complete, their .then() callback tries to call setState on an unmounted component — React warns about this (memory leak in older versions, no-op in newer). AbortController.abort() cancels the request, triggering an AbortError that you explicitly ignore in the catch block. The cleanup function (`return () => controller.abort()`) runs when the component unmounts or when the effect's dependencies change.

faq.q: Should I use React Query or write my own loading state logic?
faq.a: For any real application, use React Query (TanStack Query) or SWR. They handle: caching (no duplicate requests for the same data), background refetching, stale-while-revalidate, retry logic, pagination, optimistic updates, and the three-state pattern — all out of the box. Writing it manually works for learning but doesn't scale. React Query's core bundle is ~12kb gzipped — a worthwhile investment for every app that talks to an API.

examples: GitHub — skeleton screens while loading repo data, retry button on error
Twitter/X — optimistic like button (increments immediately, reverts if server rejects)
Notion — shows cached data instantly, fetches fresh in background (stale-while-revalidate)
